quality_rules: One SPHEREx image is poor when the pixel at the target is saturated (OVERFLOW), blank, outside the image or carries a flag that makes a pixel unusable; caution when the target pixel is fine but another pixel within 3 pixels of the target is flagged or blank (that image is then left out of the spectrum); otherwise good.

A stacked frame is poor when at least half of its images are poor, or the stacked picture is blank at the target; caution when any image is saturated at the target, at least a quarter are poor, at least half have flagged or blank pixels within 3 pixels of the target, or an image did not pass the SPHEREx pipeline's own quality check (L2DQAFLG); otherwise good. A frame of one image takes that image's verdict.

The combined frame is poor when at least half of its detector co-adds are poor; caution when any co-add is poor, any image is saturated at the target, or at least half of the co-adds need caution; otherwise good.

WISE and NEOWISE frames come without flag planes here, so only blank pixels and a saturated (blanked) core are checked: poor when the core is saturated or the target pixel is blank, caution when a pixel within 3 pixels of the target is blank.

combined.label: All 6 detectors combined (0.75–5.0 µm)
combined.method: Each detector's co-add of a visit is background-subtracted and divided by its own robust noise (median and 1.4826 x MAD); the co-adds are then summed and divided by the square root of their number, so the picture is in units of the noise and no detector dominates. It mixes wavelengths, so motion is still measured at 3.4 and 4.6 µm only.

gaia_facts.note: Not in Gaia DR3; parallax from Luhman & Esplin 2016, AJ 152, 78

items.reason: Wrong pairing: one end is the mission target, the other end is a different dot.
The 2010 end sits on a Gaia star that does not move. The dot is that star, seen in one image and missed in the other.
The SPHEREx end sits on a Gaia star that does not move. The dot is that star, seen in one image and missed in the other.
An end is at the edge of the picture, where a dot can appear or vanish without moving.

changes.method: Dots seen only in WISE 2010 are paired with dots seen only in SPHEREx at 4.6 µm, 8″ to 190″ apart and of similar brightness. Each pair is then checked against the target's path, Gaia DR3 and SIMBAD.
changes.not_checked: Asteroids and comets are not checked. An unconfirmed pair is not a discovery.

checks.text: Measured speed matches the catalogue: 8.27 vs 8.15″/yr (difference 1.5%)
No Gaia DR3 counterpart: too faint or too cold for Gaia's visible-light camera. Catalogued in the literature (Luhman & Esplin 2016, AJ 152, 78).
5.1× brighter at 4–4.75 µm than in the 3.3 µm methane band: the methane dip of a cold brown dwarf (a normal star would be below 1×)

facts.headline: About 87 km/s across the sky
facts.detail: That is 2.9 times the speed of Earth around the Sun. It is sideways speed only: motion toward or away from us does not show in images.

facts.headline: Crosses the width of the full Moon in about 220 years
facts.detail: A typical star in these images needs more than 100,000 years, which is why this one stands out in a flipbook.

facts.headline: 7.3 light-years away: one of the Sun's nearest neighbours
facts.detail: The light in these images left it about 7.3 years ago.

facts.headline: Cold enough to hold methane gas
facts.detail: Methane survives only in atmospheres below roughly 1,300 K, cooler than any true star. It absorbs light near 3.3 µm, which is why this object is 5.1× brighter at 4–4.75 µm.
facts.basis: SPHEREx flux at 4–4.75 µm ÷ flux at 3.3 µm

facts.headline: Invisible to Gaia's visible-light camera
facts.detail: It shows up only in infrared light. Objects like this are what an infrared survey can find and a visible-light survey cannot.
facts.basis: no Gaia DR3 source at the predicted position

limits: Motion: an object must shift 2 SPHEREx pixels (12″) to count as moving. Over these 15.8 years that means faster than 0.78″ per year. Slower objects read as “no measurable motion”.
SPHEREx alone covers only 12 months here: by the same 2-pixel rule, enough only for motion faster than 12″ per year. The 2010 WISE image is what makes slower motion visible.
Brightness: compared at 3 SPHEREx visits only. A change between or outside those dates is not seen.
Solar System: the page checks against Gaia stars only. It does not check asteroids or comets, so a moving dot without a Gaia circle may be a known asteroid.
Crowding: one SPHEREx pixel is 6.15″ wide, so two close objects can blend into one dot and one spectrum.
